newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Mexico, Centam see free trade deals in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Mexico, Centam see free trade deals in 1997.

text.p: Free trade negotiators from Mexico, Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador meeting in Guatemala this week said on Thursday they will come to the table again in November and could sign a treaty by next year.

"The spirits of all sides to collaborate and move forward is very positive. God willing we will sign it in the coming year," Gustavo Saravia, chief negotiator for Guatemala, said during a news conference.
During a two-day work meeting, Mexico and the so-called Northern Triangle countries of Central America, negotiating as a block, exchanged information and presented proposals for further talks.
Negotiators gave reporters no details on proposals and painted a rosy picture of negotiations so far.
Saravia said the tough details on specific products, such as beef and sugar, and rules of origin, will be addressed in the next meeting, in Mexico City on November 4 and 5.
Rules of origin are a key point for the Central American nations, with fewer raw materials than Mexico.
Saravia did not confirm earlier reports that Central America request free trade status for products assembled or manufactured in the region but containing less than 60 percent of regional materials.
The Central American nations all have trade deficits with Mexico. Imports are 18 times exports in the case of Honduras, 12 to one for El Salvador and eight to one for Guatemala.

The Northern Triangle countries are working to create unified commerce laws and tarrifs to make negotiations with Mexico simpler. Guatemala and El Salvador, for example, are already working on a bilateral free-trade treaty.
Mexico already has a free trade treaty with Costa Rica, and is in separate free trade negotiations with Nicaragua which could join the Northern Triangle negotiating block.
